paper.authors_full: Marek Urban, Filip Děchtěrenko, Jiří Lukavský, Veronika Hrabalová, Filip Svacha, Cyril Brom, Kamila Urban
paper.title: ChatGPT improves creative problem-solving performance in university students: An experimental study
paper.pdf_filename: Urban et al (2024) - ChatGPT improves creative problem-solving performance in university students.pdf
paper.version_read: Author accepted manuscript for Computers & Education, dated March 9th, 2024; the cover states this is not the copy of record (PDF p. 1).
paper.one_line_finding: Students randomly assigned to solve the Product Improvement Task with ChatGPT received higher expert ratings than students without it on quality (3.60 vs 2.99, d = 0.69), elaboration (2.79 vs 2.21, d = 0.61), and originality (2.74 vs 2.21, d = 0.55), all p < .001 (77 vs 68 students analyzed; means, d, and p in Table 2, p. 16; Ns in Table 1, p. 11).
paper.shared_samples: Urban et al. (2025), 'Prompting for creative problem-solving: A process-mining study', Learning and Instruction 99, 102156 (atlas candidate c594). It analyzes the 77 experimental-arm participants of this study: the coded transcripts of their ChatGPT conversations and the expert ratings of their PIT solutions, with the same weighted kappas (.88, .93, .85). It has no no-AI arm. Its sample description matches this paper's Table 1 experimental column on N, sex (24 men, 53 women), mean age (22.4), study subject (57, 17, 3), and level (53 undergraduates, 24 graduates), but it prints age SD 4.5 where Table 1 prints 4.1. This PDF predates c594 and names no other paper that uses its sample. Codebook section 2 gives the two papers one sample. c594 is not in retrieval.json and was read in its PsyArXiv preprint, not its journal version.

studies.label: Lab experiment: Product Improvement Task with vs. without ChatGPT
studies.cluster_se_treatment: No session clustering is reported. Students were individually randomized before the experiment, but the two conditions ran in separate sessions. The t-tests and ANCOVAs treat participants as independent (PDF pp. 10 and 16).

counts_source.locator: PDF p. 11, Participants and Table 1 headers; analyzed arm counts only
counts_source.quote: The control group for the present study contained 68 university students and the experimental group contained 77 participants

arms.name: Experimental (ChatGPT)
arms.description: Solved the Product Improvement Task with ChatGPT-3.5 (Plus) open in a second browser tab, following a short description with example prompts and responses. Task instructions explicitly referred to ChatGPT assistance. Participants also answered additional self-efficacy questions (PDF pp. 10, 13).

arms.name: Control (no ChatGPT)
arms.description: Solved the same Product Improvement Task in a single browser tab without ChatGPT. Both conditions could access additional browser tools, but no participant did so (PDF p. 10).

studies.task: Generate three original and useful improvements to an ordinary stuffed bunny to help Mattel achieve higher sales than the Lego Group (PDF pp. 12-13).

ai_tool.name: ChatGPT-3.5 (Plus)
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 10, Experimental Procedure; model/product release year is not stated.

estimates.measure_detail: Quality is the extent to which answers meet the goals of improving the bunny and increasing sales. open_items: The source prints arm sizes but no combined analyzed total. Study n_analyzed and estimate n_total are null rather than computed by summing the arms. The reconciled screening form gives a combined total, but it is not printed in this manuscript.

The paper states individual random assignment before the experiment and no exclusions, but does not print counts at assignment, the randomization mechanism, or the number of assigned volunteers who did not attend. Randomized counts remain null.

PIT score construction is incomplete: the paper does not identify the PIT raters or explain how their ratings and the three solutions become one participant score. The inferential analyses support participant-level coding, but the aggregation procedure remains unspecified.
The arms ran in separate sessions with at most five people per session. Session counts and scheduling are unreported; no adjustment for session clustering is described.

The manuscript names no primary outcome or ranking among the preregistered H1 dimensions (PDF pp. 8-9). The OSF registration was not used as a source for this reconciliation; preregistered_primary remains not_stated.
No model release year is printed. The tool name is retained verbatim from the Methods, and ai_tool.year is null.
The manuscript does not specify the standardizer for its reported d values. The unadjusted records retain the printed participant-level arm SDs.
Adjusted ANCOVA arm means, differences, SEs, coefficients, and confidence limits are not printed. The group-by-task analysis likewise lacks change summaries and a complete model specification.
Figure 1 presents z-score means and confidence bars without numerical labels. No values were digitized or inferred from the graph.
The journal version of record is not the PDF on file; the extraction is limited to the accepted manuscript and its included appendix.

review_corrections.basis: PDF p. 10: 'The experiment was held in a quiet room with a maximum of five participants at one time. The control group and experimental groups had separate sessions.' Every session ran one arm, so under the codebook section 3 session rule (added during Phase 2, 2026-10-10, for review) the session is the assignment unit. The number of sessions is not printed (clusters_per_arm stays null). The t-tests and ANCOVAs treat participants as independent, so these records are not pooled while the rule stands.

Sum of the printed analyzed arm counts (77 + 68), between-person design: 'The control group for the present study contained 68 university students and the experimental group contained 77 participants' (PDF p. 11, Participants); no exclusions (PDF p. 10). The paper prints no total; the counts pass (extraction/checks/c123.counts.json) found none either.
